title: What can we expect
lead: Linear algebra begins with sets of linear equations. Working from a few equations in two or three unknowns, drawn as lines in the plane and planes in space, this section asks what points a set of equations can have in common, and fixes the words linear equation, linear system, solution and solution space.
summary_html:
The point of this section is to build some intuition about the behavior of solutions to linear systems through consideration of some simple examples. We will develop a deeper and more precise understanding of these phenomena in our future explorations.

  • A linear equation is one that may be written in the form $a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 + \ldots + a_nx_n = b$.
  • A linear system is a set of linear equations and a solution is a set of values assigned to the unknowns that make each equation true.
  • We came to expect that a linear system has either infinitely many solutions, exactly one solution, or no solutions.
  • When we add more equations to a system, the solution space usually seems to become smaller.

exercises.prompt:
In this activity, we consider sets of linear equations having just two unknowns. In this case, we can graph the solutions sets for the equations, which allows us to visualize different types of behavior.

  1. On the grid below, graph the lines $$ \begin{aligned} y & = x+1 \\ y & = 2x-1\text{.} \end{aligned} $$ At what point or points $(x,y)$, do the lines intersect? How many points $(x,y)$ satisfy both equations?
  2. On the grid below, graph the lines $$ \begin{aligned} y & = x+1 \\ y & = x-1\text{.} \end{aligned} $$ At what point or points $(x,y)$, do the lines intersect? How many points $(x,y)$ satisfy both equations?
  3. On the grid below, graph the line $$ y = x+1 . $$ How many points $(x,y)$ satisfy this equation?
  4. On the grid below, graph the lines $$ \begin{aligned} y & = x+1 \\ y & = 2x-1 \\ y & = -x. \end{aligned} $$ At what point or points $(x,y)$, do the lines intersect? How many points $(x,y)$ satisfy all three equations?

answer.solution:
1. The graph of the two lines is as shown on the right. There is a single point, the point $(2,3)$, at which the lines intersect. Therefore, there is a single point that satisfies both equations.
  2. These two lines are parallel, which means there is no point at which the lines intersect. Therefore, there is no point that satisfies both equations.
  3. There are infinitely many points that lie on this line and that, therefore, satisfy this single equation.
  4. These three lines do not have a common intersection point. Consequently, there is no point satisfying all three equations.

exercises.prompt:
This activity considers sets of equations having three unknowns. In this case, we know that the solutions of a single equation form a plane. If it helps with visualization, consider using $3\times5$-inch index cards to represent planes.

  1. Is it possible that there are no solutions to two linear equations in three unknowns? Either sketch an example or state a reason why it can’t happen.
  2. Is it possible that there is exactly one solution to two linear equations in three unknowns? Either sketch an example or state a reason why it can’t happen.
  3. Is it possible that the solutions to four equations in three unknowns form a line? Either sketch an example or state a reason why it can’t happen.
  4. What would you usually expect for the set of solutions to four equations in three unknowns?
  5. Suppose we have a set of 500 linear equations in 10 unknowns. Which of the three possibilities would you expect to hold?
  6. Suppose we have a set of 10 linear equations in 500 unknowns. Which of the three possibilities would you expect to hold?

answer.solution:
1. Yes, it is possible if the two planes are parallel to one another.
  2. No, this is not possible. Two planes will either intersect in a line, if they are not parallel, or not intersect at all, if they are parallel.
  3. Yes, it is possible that four planes intersect in a line. One may sketch four planes that intersect in, say, the $z$-axis.
  4. In general, we would expect there to be no solutions to four equations in three unknowns because there are more equations than unknowns.
  5. Since there are more equations than unknowns, we would expect there to be no solutions. We cannot guarantee this, however.
  6. Since there are fewer equations than unknowns, we would expect there to be infinitely many solutions. We cannot guarantee this, however.

exercises.prompt:
1. Which of the following equations are linear? Please provide a justification for your response.
    1. $2x + xy -3y^2 = 2$.
    2. $-2x_1 + 3x_2 +4x_3 - x_5 = 0$.
    3. $x = 3z - 4y$.
  2. Consider the system of linear equations: $$ \begin{alignedat}{4} x & {}+{} & y & & & {}={} & 3 \\ & & y & {}-{} & z & {}={} & 2 \\ 2x & {}+{} & y & {}+{} & z & {}={} & 4. \end{alignedat} $$
    1. Is $(x,y,z) = (1,2,0)$ a solution?
    2. Is $(x,y,z) = (-2,1,0)$ a solution?
    3. Is $(x,y,z) = (0,-3,1)$ a solution?
    4. Can you find a solution in which $y = 0$?
    5. Do you think there are other solutions? Please explain your response.

answer.solution:
1. There are two linear equations in this list.
    1. This is not a linear equation due to the presence of $y^2$ in the third term on the left.
    2. This is a linear equation.
    3. This is a linear equation since it can be rewritten in the form $x + 4y - 3z = 0$.
  2. We will see that the system of linear equations has infinitely many solutions.
    1. Yes, this is a solution since all three equations are satisfied if we set $x=1$, $y=2$, and $z=0$.
    2. No, this is not a solution since the first equation is not satisfied if $x=-2$ and $y=1$.
    3. This is also not a solution.
    4. If $y=0$, then we arrive at the system of three linear equations: $$ \begin{alignedat}{4} x & & & {}={} & 3 \\ & {}-{} & z & {}={} & 2 \\ 2x & {}+{} & z & {}={} & 4. \end{alignedat} $$ We have a solution when $x=3$ and $z=-2$. Therefore, $(x,y,z)=(3,0,-2)$ is a solution to the original system of equations.
    5. Since we have found more than one solution to the system of equations, we should expect that there are infinitely many. Therefore, there should be many other solutions.

exercises.prompt:
Give a brief explanation of your response to the following questions.

  1. Suppose we have a system of 500 linear equations in 10 unknowns. What would be a reasonable guess about which of the three possibilities for the set of solutions holds?
  2. Suppose we have a system of 10 linear equations in 500 unknowns. What would be a reasonable guess about which of the three possibilities for the set of solutions holds?

answer.solution:
Each equation adds a condition on the unknowns, so the more equations a system has, the smaller its set of solutions usually is.

  1. There are far more equations than unknowns, so we would expect no solutions: ten unknowns can satisfy ten well-chosen conditions, and the other 490 equations usually ask for something those ten values cannot do, just as a third line in the plane usually misses the point where two others meet. We cannot guarantee this, however; the 500 equations could happen to agree.
  2. There are far fewer equations than unknowns, so we would expect infinitely many solutions: ten conditions leave most of the 500 unknowns free, just as one equation in two unknowns leaves a whole line of points. We cannot guarantee this either, since the equations could be inconsistent, as two parallel lines are.

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following equations are linear? Please provide a justification for your response.

  1. $2x + xy -3y^2 = 2$.
  2. $-2x_1 + 3x_2 +4x_3 - x_5 = 0$.
  3. $x = 3z - 4y$.

answer.solution:
An equation is linear when it can be written as $a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 + \ldots + a_nx_n = b$, every term on the left a constant times the first power of one unknown.

  1. Not linear: the term $xy$ multiplies two unknowns and the term $-3y^2$ has $y$ to the second power, so neither is a constant times the first power of an unknown.
  2. Linear: it already has the form $a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 + a_3x_3 + a_5x_5 = 0$ with coefficients $-2$, $3$, $4$ and $-1$ (the unknown $x_4$ simply has coefficient $0$).
  3. Linear: moving the unknowns to one side gives $x + 4y - 3z = 0$, which has the required form with coefficients $1$, $4$ and $-3$.

So two of the three equations are linear.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the system of linear equations:

$$ \begin{alignedat}{4} x & {}+{} & y & & & {}={} & 3 \\ & & y & {}-{} & z & {}={} & 2 \\ 2x & {}+{} & y & {}+{} & z & {}={} & 4. \end{alignedat} $$
  1. Is $(x,y,z) = (1,2,0)$ a solution?
  2. Is $(x,y,z) = (-2,1,0)$ a solution?
  3. Is $(x,y,z) = (0,-3,1)$ a solution?
  4. Can you find a solution in which $y = 0$?
  5. Do you think there are other solutions? Please explain your response.

answer.solution:
A set of values is a solution when it satisfies all three equations, so we substitute it into each.

  1. Yes. With $x=1$, $y=2$, $z=0$: $1 + 2 = 3$, $2 - 0 = 2$ and $2(1) + 2 + 0 = 4$, so all three equations hold.
  2. No. With $x=-2$, $y=1$: the first equation gives $-2 + 1 = -1 eq 3$, so it fails, and one failed equation is enough.
  3. No. With $x=0$, $y=-3$: the first equation gives $0 + (-3) = -3 eq 3$ (and the second gives $-3 - 1 = -4 eq 2$).
  4. Yes. Setting $y = 0$ leaves $x = 3$, $-z = 2$ and $2x + z = 4$. The first two give $x = 3$ and $z = -2$, and the third is then $2(3) + (-2) = 4$, which holds. So $(x,y,z) = (3,0,-2)$ is a solution.
  5. Yes. We have already found two different solutions, $(1,2,0)$ and $(3,0,-2)$, and by the three possibilities a system with more than one solution has infinitely many. Indeed, for any value $t$ of $y$, $x = 3 - t$ and $z = t - 2$ satisfy all three equations: $(3 - t) + t = 3$, $t - (t - 2) = 2$ and $2(3 - t) + t + (t - 2) = 4$.

exercises.prompt:
This exercise concerns systems of equations having three unknowns. In this case, we know that the solution space of a single equation is a plane. If it helps with visualization, consider using $3\times5$ index cards to represent planes.

  1. Is it possible that the solution space of a system of four equations in three unknowns is a line? Either sketch an example or give a reason why it can’t happen.
  2. What would you usually expect for the solution space to a system of four equations in three unknowns?
  3. Is it possible that there are no solutions to a system of two equations in three unknowns? Either sketch an example or give a reason why it can’t happen.
  4. Is it possible that there is exactly one solution to a system of two equations in three unknowns? Either sketch an example or give a reason why it can’t happen.

answer.solution:
Each equation’s solution space is a plane, and the solution space of the system is where all of its planes meet.

  1. Yes. Four planes can all pass through one line, like the pages of an open book sharing its spine: the planes $y = 0$, $x = 0$, $x = y$ and $x = -y$ all contain the $z$-axis, so the system of those four equations has the $z$-axis as its solution space.
  2. We would usually expect no solutions. Three planes typically meet in a single point, and a fourth plane usually misses that point, since there are more equations than unknowns.
  3. Yes. Two parallel planes, such as $z = 0$ and $z = 1$, have no point in common, so the system of those two equations has no solutions.
  4. No. Two planes either are parallel, with no point in common, or meet along a whole line; two planes can never meet in just one point. So two equations in three unknowns have either no solutions or infinitely many, never exactly one.
